title: Pangolin-Associated Viruses: Diversity, Evolutionary Adaptation, and Zoonotic Spillover Risks.
abstract: Pangolin-associated viruses have received considerable attention because of their diversity and potential zoonotic relevance, yet the evidence remains fragmented. This review evaluates the diversity, evolutionary adaptation, and zoonotic spillover risks of pangolin-associated viruses. Diverse RNA and DNA viruses, such as coronaviruses, paramyxoviruses, astroviruses, parvoviruses, and papillomaviruses, have been detected in pangolins, showing substantial taxonomic and genomic variation. Studies of selected pangolin-associated viral groups have documented sequence variation and identified signals of recombination or reassortment. Some pangolin coronaviruses can use human receptors and replicate in human-derived cells, organoids, or transgenic animal models. Several viruses known to infect humans have also been detected in pangolin samples, although conclusive evidence of natural spillover from pangolins to humans is lacking. Most studies examine Sunda and Chinese pangolins from illegal trade or rescue centers, relying largely on nucleic acid detection and sequence analysis. Habitat disruption, wildlife trafficking, long-distance transport and captive-rescue operations may increase cross-host-pathogen exposure. Future work should prioritize surveillance of wild pangolin populations of known provenance and integrate virus isolation, tissue localization, serology, and functional assays to support pangolin conservation and reliable zoonotic-risk evaluation.

title: Emerging and Novel Ovine Viruses: Molecular Diagnostics, Genomic and Metagenomic Surveillance, and One Health Perspectives.
abstract: Emerging and novel ovine viruses pose increasing threats to animal health, livestock productivity, trade, food security, and public health preparedness. Their emergence is driven by complex interactions among animal movement, mixed-species production systems, wildlife-livestock interfaces, arthropod vectors, environmental changes, and viral evolution. This review critically compares current strategies for identifying major, emerging, re-emerging, zoonotic, and newly recognized ovine viruses, with emphasis on their analytical sensitivity, turnaround time, throughput, operational cost, accessibility, field applicability, validation status, and capacity for novel-virus detection. Conventional diagnostic approaches, including virus isolation, serology, antigen detection, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry, remain essential for confirmation and flock-level surveillance but may be limited by slow turnaround, dependence on specialized facilities, reduced sensitivity at low viral loads, and an inability to identify highly divergent or unknown viruses. Targeted molecular assays, including PCR, RT-PCR, qPCR, multiplex assays, digital PCR, isothermal amplification, and CRISPR-based diagnostics, have improved detection speed and sensitivity but generally require prior knowledge of viral genomic targets. Genomic and metagenomic approaches, including whole-genome sequencing, next-generation sequencing, nanopore sequencing, viral metagenomics, bioinformatics, and phylogenetic analysis, provide broader detection capabilities by enabling characterization of viral diversity, outbreak tracing, co-infection identification, and discovery of previously unrecognized viruses. However, their interpretation remains challenging due to low viral abundance, poor sample quality, host nucleic acid background, contamination, incomplete reference databases, limited computational capacity, and the inability of sequence detection alone to confirm disease causality. Therefore, future ovine virus surveillance requires integration of molecular diagnostics with active, passive, outbreak-based, risk-based, vector, wildlife, and animal-movement surveillance within a One Health framework. Linking genomic information with ecological, epidemiological, and environmental data will be essential for transforming ovine virus surveillance from reactive diagnosis toward proactive preparedness. Advances in standardized sampling, validated field diagnostics, affordable sequencing, curated databases, bioinformatics capacity, and cross-sector data sharing will strengthen early recognition, risk assessment, and preparedness against emerging viral threats in sheep.

title: Comprehensive Identification and Description of Mitochondrial DNA Haplogroups and Sub-Haplogroups in Snow Sheep (
abstract: Mitochondrial DNA is a powerful marker for reconstructing maternal lineages and phylogeographic history in wild species. The snow sheep (Ovis nivicola), a mountain ungulate endemic to Siberia and the Russian Far East, is characterized by strong geographic fragmentation and a complex taxonomic structure. A formal mitochondrial haplogroup classification system for the species has, however, been lacking. In this study, we sequenced and analyzed 257 complete mitochondrial genomes representing all major populations across the species' range. Using phylogenetic reconstruction and diagnostic mutations (present in 100% of individuals within clades), we identified four major haplogroups (A-D) and multiple nested sub-haplogroups with clear geographic structuring. Divergence times were estimated using Bayesian analysis in BEAST 2.7.7 with a relaxed lognormal clock model, calibrated by the divergence between O. dalli and O. canadensis. The results showed that haplogroup A is almost exclusive to Kamchatka, haplogroup B is predominant in northern populations, haplogroup C is the most widespread and diverse across the species range, and haplogroup D is largely restricted to the Verkhoyansk region. The mitochondrial data largely support traditional subspecies taxonomy but reveal mitochondrial polyphyly in some subspecies, particularly O. n. lydekkeri and O. n. koriakorum. This study provides the first comprehensive mitochondrial haplogroup system for snow sheep and shows that the observed mitochondrial phylogeographic patterns are consistent with an important influence of Pleistocene glacial cycles and prolonged geographic isolation on its current genetic structure. These findings offer important insights for conservation management and for understanding the evolutionary history of wild sheep in Northeast Asia.

title: Zoonotic Viral Spillover: From Reservoir Ecology and Viral Evolution to Pandemic Prevention.
abstract: Zoonotic viral spillover represents a major global health challenge arising from complex interactions among viral evolution, reservoir ecology, host biology, environmental disruption, and human activities. Successful emergence requires viruses to overcome successive ecological, cellular, and immunological barriers, including receptor compatibility, cellular tropism, replication efficiency, and innate immune restriction. Reservoir hosts such as bats, rodents, birds, and livestock contribute to viral maintenance and diversification through distinct ecological and physiological characteristics, while deforestation, agricultural expansion, wildlife trade, intensive farming, urbanization, and climate variability can increase opportunities for cross-species transmission. Following spillover, viral adaptation and host susceptibility determine whether infections remain sporadic or progress to sustained human transmission. This review integrates ecological, molecular, immunological, and anthropogenic determinants of zoonotic emergence and examines major historical spillover events involving coronaviruses, influenza viruses, filoviruses, henipaviruses, and arboviruses. We further evaluate genomic and metagenomic surveillance, wastewater monitoring, artificial intelligence, ecological modeling, and integrated One Health approaches for early risk assessment and pandemic preparedness. Major knowledge gaps include limited characterization of global viral diversity, surveillance bias, inadequate functional validation of newly identified viruses, fragmented data systems, and limited predictive capacity. Future prevention requires integration of technological innovation with ecological conservation, equitable surveillance capacity, responsible biotechnology governance, and sustainable One Health Planetary Health strategies.

title: High prevalence of hypervirulent Staphylococcus aureus CC22-t309 in Pediatric Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis in China.
abstract: This study aimed to elucidate the molecular epidemiology, virulence factors, and antimicrobial resistance profiles of Staphylococcus aureus isolated from children with osteomyelitis and septic arthritis (OM-SA) in China. A total of 68 S. aureus isolates were collected from pediatric patients with OM-SA in Shanghai, China, with 100 strains from children with other infections serving as controls. We performed a systematic analysis on all strains by integrating clinical metadata, whole-genome sequencing, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Among S. aureus isolates from OM-SA cases, CC22-t309 was the dominant clone (32.3%), followed by CC59-t437 (17.6%). The prevalence of CC22-t309 in OM-SA was much higher than that in the control (32.3% vs. 8.0%, p<0.001). OM-SA patients with CC22-t309 infection presented much higher inflammatory markers than those infected with other clones (p<0.05). Notably, CC22-t309 from OM-SA exhibited higher carriage of virulence factors, including Panton-Valentine leukocidin (pvl, 100%), collagen adhesin (cna, 86.4%), and fibronectin-binding proteins (fnbA/B, 77.3%), compared with other clones (pvl, 0∼66.7%; cna, 0∼13.8%; fnbA/B, 0∼24.1%; p < 0.05). Within CC22-t309 clone, the carriage of pvl, fnbB and fnbA showed no difference between OM-SA and control group (pvl: 100% vs. 87.5%; fnbB: 77.3% vs. 85.7%; fnbA: 77.3% vs. 37.5%; p >0.05). However, the prevalence of cna in OM-SA was significantly higher than that in the control group (86.4% vs. 37.5%, p = 0.015). Furthermore, CC22-t309 isolates displayed a multidrug-resistant phenotype against β-lactams, macrolides, and lincosamides. We identify the hypervirulent and multidrug-resistant CC22-t309 as a high-risk S. aureus lineage associated with pediatric OM-SA.

title: Antimicrobial Resistance and Molecular Epidemiology of Enterococcus Species Isolated at the University Hospitals of Sfax, Tunisia.
abstract: Enterococci are major causes of both community-acquired and healthcare-associated infections. The rapid global dissemination of multidrug-resistant clones poses a major challenge to clinical management and infection control. The aim for the present study was to investigate the prevalence, antimicrobial resistance patterns, virulence genes, and molecular epidemiology of Enterococcus species isolated from clinical specimens in university hospitals of Sfax, Tunisia. A descriptive, hospital-based, cross-sectional surveillance study was conducted between March 2020 and February 2021. It included all Enterococcus strains isolated in the Microbiology Department of Habib Bourguiba University Hospital. Enterococcus isolates were tested for antimicrobial susceptibility in accordance with European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing guidelines. Polymerase chain reaction assays were performed to detect resistance genes (vanA, vanB, ermA, ermB, ermC, msrA, mefE, vga, vat, vgb), virulence genes (gelatinase [gelE], aggregation substance, enterococcal surface protein [esp], cytolysin, hyaluronidase), and the IS16 marker associated with the clonal complex 17 (CC17) lineage. A total of 231 Enterococcus isolates were recovered, including Enterococcus faecalis (62.3%) and Enterococcus faecium (34.2%). All E. faecalis isolates were susceptible to ampicillin, vancomycin, and linezolid; all E. faecium isolates were resistant to ampicillin, and 7.6% exhibited vanA-mediated glycopeptide resistance. The ermB gene was the predominant macrolide resistance determinant. Among E. faecium, esp (74.7%) was the most prevalent virulence gene, whereas E. faecalis mainly harbored gelE (78.5%). The IS16 element, characteristic of CC17 clones, was detected in 86.1% of E. faecium isolates. The present study highlights the emergence of multidrug-resistant E. faecium strains with molecular features suggestive of CC17 affiliation in hospital settings in Sfax, Tunisia, underscoring the urgent need for stronger infection control and antimicrobial stewardship programs.

title: Mapping the frontiers of genomic disease surveillance research in the ASEAN region: scientometric insights for precision public health and next-generation epidemic intelligence.
abstract: Genomic disease surveillance has become a cornerstone of precision public health, yet the regional research architecture in Southeast Asia remains insufficiently characterized. This study provides a comprehensive scientometric mapping of genomic surveillance research in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) region and identifies patterns relevant to the development of epidemic intelligence systems. A scientometric analysis of 8129 Scopus-indexed publications (2000-25) was conducted using Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny and VOSviewer software. Analyses included publication trends, citation patterns, collaboration networks, institutional productivity, funding sources, keyword co-occurrence, and thematic evolution. The field demonstrates robust annual growth (14.49%) and high international collaboration (43.92%). Thailand, led by Mahidol and Chulalongkorn Universities, emerged as the principal regional knowledge hub in terms of indexed scholarly visibility. Publication influence is concentrated in a limited set of high-impact journals (PLOS One, Emerging Infectious Diseases, Journal of Clinical Microbiology) and internationally connected author networks. Thematic evolution reveals a transition from molecular epidemiology toward whole-genome sequencing (WGS), antimicrobial resistance (AMR), zoonotic surveillance, and One Health intelligence. Growth modeling suggests sustained expansion through the early 2040s. Genomic disease surveillance research in Southeast Asia has grown substantially, with expanding international collaboration and thematic shifts toward WGS, AMR, zoonotic surveillance, and One Health. However, research output remains concentrated in a few countries and institutions, and bibliometric findings do not measure surveillance capacity or policy implementation. Further research integrating laboratory, funding, epidemiological, and policy evidence is needed across ASEAN.

title: Scaling of SARS-CoV-2 Genomic Divergence with Cumulative COVID-19 Infections.
abstract: The rate at which viral lineages accumulate genetic divergence is central to understanding pathogen evolution, yet direct empirical measurements are limited. The COVID-19 pandemic, through the combination of pandemic-scale replication and dense genomic surveillance, offers an opportunity to calibrate this relationship directly. Unlike previous analyses that use time as the independent variable, this study uses cumulative infections, providing an epidemiological clock calibrated in units of replication opportunity that is not confounded by variation in transmission intensity. A total of 1279 SARS-CoV-2 genomes from the Nextstrain open dataset, sampled between February 2020 and February 2023, were paired with contemporaneous estimates of cumulative global infections from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) to model genomic divergence from Wuhan-Hu-1 as a function of cumulative infections. Divergence increased sublinearly across roughly 14 billion infections over three years, with the most diverged circulating genomes accumulating only about 120 substitutions relative to Wuhan-Hu-1. Extrapolating the fitted relationships, generating the roughly 1000 substitutions that separate SARS-CoV-2 from its closest known sarbecovirus relatives would require on the order of 100-300 billion human infection-equivalents. These requirements would increase substantially in wildlife reservoir hosts, where viral replication per infection is orders of magnitude lower. Conservative estimates of the replication opportunity available in Rhinolophus bat populations imply that the common ancestor of SARS-CoV-2 and its nearest sequenced relatives predates modern virological surveillance by roughly a century. More realistic estimates raise this estimate to millennia, suggesting the closest known relatives of SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 cannot have served as their progenitors.
